title: The battle inside
hook: the fiercest fight in the Granth is with the five thieves in your own mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nihang orders, and your line, the old ways kept. A week of swords, flags and horsemen. Today, the last day of sword and saint, and the fight the Guru Granth Sahib keeps coming back to. Day two hundred eighty-one.

No army, no siege, no broken oath. Just an ordinary day that went wrong from the inside: a snapped word at someone loved, an hour scrolled away that wasn't there to spare, a grab for the bigger slice, the last word, the credit. For a week this path has talked about swords. Open the Guru Granth Sahib looking for battles, though, and the ones it keeps returning to have no armies in them. Its fiercest fight happens somewhere else. Today: the battle inside.
screen: `NO ARMY, NO SIEGE.` → `A DAY LOST FROM THE INSIDE.` → `THE FIERCEST FIGHT IS ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: The Granth names the enemy many times, and it has five faces: kaam, desire that grabs; krodh, anger; lobh, greed; moh, clinging to what we can't keep; and ahankar, pride. We met these five thieves weeks ago. Today, the line that turns them into a battle. It's in Guru Nanak's Japji, the morning prayer, in the twenty-eighth verse. That verse speaks to the yogis of Guru Nanak's day and turns their outward gear inward: make contentment your earrings, meditation the ash on your body, faith your staff. Then it closes on a short line: man jeetai jag jeet. Conquer your own mind, and you've conquered the world. Think about what that does to everything we learned this week. The saint-soldier's courage. The kirpan, mercy first. Every other means first. Fair, even in conflict. The calm face in gatka. Every one of those depends on winning an inner fight first: against anger that wants to strike, pride that wants to win, fear that wants to run. A soldier who hasn't fought the five thieves isn't a saint-soldier, just a soldier. The Granth's weapons for this fight aren't made of steel. The Name, remembered. The company of good people, the sangat. The Guru's word. Honest work and sharing. And humility, the opposite of ahankar. Sikhs don't speak of winning it once and for all. It's a daily fight, and the wins are often small: one sharp word not said, one craving let pass. That's the battle the whole week pointed to.
screen: `THE FIVE THIEVES, MET AGAIN.` · `JAPJI 28: THE YOGI'S GEAR TURNED INWARD.` · `CONQUER THE MIND, CONQUER THE WORLD.` · `THE WEAPONS: NAME, SANGAT, HUMILITY.` · then, large: `THE REAL BATTLE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and take an honest look inward for a moment. Which of the five is loudest in you today? Anger, greed, desire, clinging, or pride? Don't fight it yet. Just name it, quietly, the way you'd name a visitor. Then choose one small win against it for later today. One word you won't say, or one thing you'll let go of. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The battle inside. The Granth's fiercest fight is with the five thieves in your own mind. Conquer the mind, and you conquer the world.
Your line: the real battle. Today, win one small inner fight: the word unsaid or the thing let go. Day two hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of the five thieves (kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, ahankar) as the real enemies, and fight them through naam simran, the sangat, the Guru's word, honest work and humility.

what a scholar hears: pauri 28 of the Japji (Ang 6) addresses yogis, recasting their earrings, ash and staff as inner virtues, and closes on man jeetai jag jeet, conquering the mind as conquering the world.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 600 (Sorath, Guru Amar Das): five thieves within the body

notes: The Gurmukhi line from Japji 28 is given in the original only; the English is a paraphrase. Confirm spelling and transliteration.

The 'five thieves in the body' image (they plunder the amrit within) is attributed to Guru Amar Das, Sorath, Ang 600; the English is a paraphrase, not a translation. Reviewer changed 'stealing the jewel of the Name' to 'plunder the nectar within' to track the original more closely. Confirm the Ang, attribution and wording.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the hook told the listener what they did ('you snapped at someone you love') and reused day 239's house-and-thieves picture; the teach repeated day 239's Ang 600 hymn and the match repeated its pairs exactly. Now the hook opens on 'no army, no siege', the teach recaps the five briefly and spends its time on Japji 28 (the yogi's earrings, ash and staff turned inward, closing on man jeetai jag jeet), and the match, practice image and trapdoor are new. The Ang 600 source stays as the ground for the five thieves.
